bodyHtml:
Sentences can be true, false, or, sometimes, truly nonsensical. For sentences of the form, “The [subject] is [predicate]”, we can divide them into “sensible” and “nonsensical” groups:

sensiblenonsensical
The moon is purple.✓The idea is purple.*
The game is an hour long.✓The pig is an hour long.*
The girl is sorry.✓The fear is sorry.*

In 1959, philosopher Fred Sommers theorized that the predicates of any language were organized in a binary tree structure, according to which subjects they could be used sensibly with. In 1979, psychologist Frank C. Keil tested Sommers’ tree theory by asking children whether given English sentences made sense or not and diagramming the results. He confirmed Sommers’ theory, producing trees like this one:

Tree diagram adapted from: Frank C. Keil. Semantic and Conceptual Development: An Ontological Perspective. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1979

Here are some English sentences that use words you may not be familiar with:

The morkle is phlebular.✓The groob is brastic.✓
The humbrid is phlebular.✓The vippage is molistic.*
The morkle is luctious.*The quexor is molistic.*
The quexor is luctious.✓The thalf is molistic.✓
The pladry is luctious.✓The humbrid is molistic.✓
The groob is efrimious.*The groob is frungent.*
The vippage is efrimious.✓The thalf is frungent.*
The pladry is frungent.*The thalf is stibbly.*
The groob is stibbly.*The groob is luctious.*

Here is a tree that shows the semantic structure of the words used in these sentences. Note that each number and letter in the tree corresponds to exactly one word.

Tree diagram typeset by Daniel Lovsted.

D1. Fill in the following table. Some of the answers have already been entered:

Predicate:brasticefrimiousfrungentluctiousmolisticphlebularstibbly
Position:G
Subject:groobhumbridmorklepladryquexorthalfvippage

D2. Mark each of the following sentences with ✓ or * again, as usual:

A. The humbrid is frungent.

B. The morkle is stibbly.

C. The pladry is phlebular.

D. The groob is molistic.

questions.partPrompt: Fill in the table: give the position in the tree (a letter for each predicate, a number for each subject). Some of the answers have already been entered: stibbly is G and quexor is 2.
Mark each of the following sentences with the check mark (sensible) or * (nonsensical).

hints.text: In the second tree, every capital letter stands for one predicate and every number stands for one subject. Before touching the tree, make two short lists for each predicate from the sentence data: the subjects it is sensible with, and the subjects it is nonsensical with.

The tree works like this: a predicate sitting at a node is sensible with exactly those numbered subjects that hang somewhere below that node, and nonsensical with all the others. So a predicate near the top is sensible with many subjects, and a predicate at the end of a branch is sensible with only one. Match the size of each predicate's sensible list against the number of leaves below each letter, and remember that if two predicates share a subject, one of their nodes must sit above the other.

Test the idea on the English tree first: "purple" sits above "tall", so anything that can be tall (a girl, a rabbit) can also be purple, while a thunderstorm sits under "an hour long" on a different branch and so cannot be purple. Now count leaves in the second tree: A has all seven numbers below it, B has five of them, D has three, and C, E, F and G each have exactly one. Those counts tell you which predicates can possibly go where before you work out any single word.

explanationHtml:
What the tree means

A predicate is the part after “is” (“... is purple”), and the subject is the thing being described. Sommers’ idea is that predicates live in a tree, and a predicate can be used sensibly with exactly those subjects that hang somewhere below it. In the English tree, “purple” sits high up, so almost anything can be purple; “wilted” sits low, so only a maple (and things near it) can wilt sensibly. A pig cannot be an hour long because “pig” is not below “an hour long”.

Reading the shape of the second tree

Letters are predicates, numbers are subjects. Counting which numbered leaves hang under each letter:

  • A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 (all seven)
  • B: 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 (five)
  • C: 3 (one)
  • D: 4, 6, 7 (three)
  • E: 5 (one)
  • F: 6 (one)
  • G: 7 (one)

So exactly one predicate works with everything, one works with five subjects, one with three, and four of them work with a single subject each.

Sorting the sentence data

From the sentences: phlebular is fine with morkle and humbrid; luctious is fine with quexor and pladry but bad with morkle and groob; molistic is fine with thalf and humbrid but bad with vippage and quexor; brastic is fine with groob; efrimious is fine with vippage but bad with groob; frungent is fine with humbrid but bad with groob, thalf and pladry; stibbly is bad with groob and thalf.

Using the two given answers

We are told quexor is 2. Leaf 2 hangs under A and B only, so a predicate that is sensible with quexor must sit at A or B, and a predicate that is nonsensical with it cannot. Since quexor is luctious, luctious is at A or B; since quexor is not molistic, molistic is neither A nor B.

Which subjects sit outside B?

Both morkle and groob reject luctious. If luctious were at A, it would work with everything, so luctious is at B, and morkle and groob must be the two leaves outside B: they are 1 and 3, in some order.

Leaf 1 has only A above it, so a subject at 1 can be sensible with just one predicate (the one at A). But groob is sensible with brastic, while morkle is sensible with phlebular, which also works with humbrid — so phlebular must cover more than one subject and therefore cannot be the single node above leaf 3 (which is C, covering only leaf 3). That forces morkle to be leaf 1, with phlebular at A, and groob to be leaf 3, with brastic at C.

Down the middle branch

molistic covers thalf and humbrid but not quexor or vippage, and it is not A or B. The only remaining node with more than one leaf is D (leaves 4, 6, 7), so molistic is D, and thalf and humbrid are two of 4, 6, 7.

frungent works with humbrid but not thalf, so it is a one-leaf node under D: F or G. We are given that stibbly is G, so frungent is F and humbrid is leaf 6. thalf is then 4 or 7, but thalf is not stibbly, and stibbly = G covers leaf 7, so thalf is 4.

The last two subjects

Only efrimious is left for node E, so efrimious is E, which covers leaf 5 alone. Since vippage is efrimious, vippage is 5, and the last remaining leaf, 7, is pladry. Check: pladry is luctious (leaf 7 does sit under B) and not frungent (7 is not under F) — both match the data.

Part D2

Now just ask whether the subject's leaf sits below the predicate's node.

  • A. humbrid is 6, frungent is F, and 6 hangs under F: sensible.
  • B. morkle is 1, stibbly is G, which covers only 7: nonsensical.
  • C. pladry is 7, phlebular is A, which covers everything: sensible.
  • D. groob is 3, molistic is D, which covers 4, 6, 7 only: nonsensical.
